sm: This part argues that carbon, water, and oxygen appear fine-tuned for life. Carbon can form a huge number of stable bonds, with more than sixty-five million compounds identified, and a speaker says anyone building complex self-replicating chemistry would have to choose it. Carbon compounds are only stable in the narrow temperature range found on Earth, unlike the heat of Venus or the cold of Uranus, and the narration says silicon-based life is considered science fiction by most experts. Water is described as a universal solvent that dissolves minerals without destroying them, unlike sulfuric acid. Its viscosity is said to be just right: lower would endanger delicate cell structures, while the discussion of higher viscosity begins as the part ends.

Slightly higher viscosity, it says, would make pumping blood through tiny capillaries impossible, so water's viscosity seems finely tuned for life. The speakers then turn to water's thermal properties. Its high heat capacity helps planets and bodies keep stable temperatures, and its very high evaporative cooling lets warm-blooded animals shed heat even when surroundings reach about thirty-eight degrees Celsius. Humans, being relatively hairless, cool by evaporation more efficiently than other mammals and can exert themselves longer in the heat. Water also expands when it freezes, so ice floats and insulates the liquid below, which keeps oceans and lakes from freezing solid. Finally, the tectonic cycle and the water cycle work together like two cogs to recycle minerals and keep Earth's surface stable for life.
